# The two gestures at the wrecked car (≈ 152.9 s – 156.0 s)

## What is happening at that point in the film

This is the American Red Cross first‑aid film **"Why Not Live?"**. A driver has
run off the road and rolled his car down an embankment (the crash montage runs
≈ 110–122 s); the car comes to rest nose‑down in the ditch with the injured
driver lying on the ground beside it.

At about **148 s** a second car — an open convertible with the top down — pulls
up on the road above. A man in a soft hat and a heavy overcoat scrambles over the
bank and runs down to the wreck (≈ 149–150.5 s). The woman who is travelling with
him stays up at the top of the bank by their car; you can actually see her
standing up there in the background at about 150.4–151 s.

The man drops to one knee beside the casualty, takes a quick look at him
(≈ 151–152.8 s), and then — **without leaving the injured man** — turns his head
back and up toward the road and signals to the woman twice.

## The two gestures, precisely

**Gesture 1 — the raised index finger (≈ 153.0 – 153.8 s).**
Still crouched over the victim, he throws his right arm up above and behind his
head, makes a fist with the **index finger extended and jabbing straight upward**,
and holds it there for the best part of a second while looking up at her.

**Gesture 2 — the outflung, pointing arm (≈ 154.6 – 156.0 s).**
He brings the arm down, glances at the casualty again, then swings the same arm
out to its **full extension, index finger pointing up and away past the wrecked
car, off along the road**, and holds that point for over a second before turning
back to the injured man.

## What the gestures mean

**Together they are a single urgent instruction: "Don't come down here — go, that
way, and get help. I'll stay with him."**

* The first gesture — the finger held up and jabbed upward — is the
  attention‑getting, emphatic half of the message: *"Stop / wait there — listen to
  me,"* and at the same time *"up there"*, i.e. get back up to the road and the
  car. It is a command, not a request for her to join him.
* The second gesture — the arm flung out at full stretch, pointing away down the
  road — is the specific, directional half: *"Go — that way!"* It tells her not
  merely to go, but which way to drive. He does not get up or go himself, which
  is the point: one person stays with the casualty, the other fetches help.

Neither gesture means "come here", "help me lift him", or "the car is on fire" —
he never beckons her toward himself, and he stays glued to the victim throughout.

## How the film confirms this reading

The payoff follows immediately and leaves no ambiguity:

* **157 – 161 s:** the woman is at their open car at the roadside; she reaches in
  over the side to the dash, then climbs into the driver's seat.
* **161 – 168 s:** the man is left alone at the bottom of the bank, kneeling over
  the injured driver, covering him and staying with him — exactly as his gestures
  said he would.
* **168 – 175 s:** her convertible speeds down the road and turns into a roadside
  Esso filling station that carries the **"EMERGENCY FIRST AID — American Red
  Cross"** sign.
* **176 – 180 s:** she talks urgently to the attendant from the driver's seat,
  gesturing back the way she has come.
* **181 – 187 s:** the attendant runs inside and **telephones for help** while she
  stands beside him; a Red Cross first‑aid crew is then dispatched to the crash
  site and takes over the care of the victim.

So the two gestures mean, in plain words: **"He's badly hurt — I'm staying with
him. You get going, back up to the car, and drive that way for help / to a
telephone."** That is precisely the lesson the film is teaching about what to do
at a highway accident: don't crowd or move the injured person, keep someone with
them, and send the other person for trained assistance.

**Short answer:** After he has run down to the wreck and checked the injured, the man stands up and signals to the woman, who has stayed up on the road by their own car. ## What is on screen (film: American Red Cross, "Why Not Live?")

- About 2:24–2:29 (144–149 s): the crashed car lies on its side in a roadside ditch with the injured occupants lying on the ground beside it.
- About 2:29–2:31 (149–151 s): a passing motorist – a man in a hat and overcoat – has stopped his open touring car on the road above. The woman is sitting in the car. He leaves her there and runs down the embankment to the wreck.

He holds the hand up, motionless, for well over a second. This is the classic "halt / wait / hold on" hand signal, also used to catch someone's attention. Its meaning here is: "Stay there – stop – don't come down; wait for my signal."
- **Second gesture, about 2:34–2:36 (154.5–156.3 s):** without lowering the arm he swings it down and out to the side and holds it extended, pointing hard away along the road (back in the direction from which they had come – the film has just shown the roadside "Emergency First Aid – American Red Cross" and "First Aid Station – American Red Cross" signs that the car passed). 1. **Raised arm / open hand held up = "Stop – wait – stay where you are."** He does not want her to come down to the wreck (there is nothing she can do there and he needs her at the car); he is getting her attention and telling her to hold on.
